item.title: About
item.description:
About

A brief introduction to the experiences and education that have taught me how to reduce costs and improving quality with data.

My Approach

Hello! I'm Jim Lehner, a manufacturing and process improvement engineer who specializes in reducing costs and improving the quality of manufactured products by leveraging industry's most valuable, yet underutilized, resource: data.

Data has become the currency of our time, yet few know what to do with it. As a result, much of what passes for analysis is little more than simple comparisons. Such an approach compares a current value with a past value, a target value, or a descriptive statistic. When the current value is not as "good" as it should be, whatever that means, explanations are required and reports must be written. A root cause must be identified and control plans put in place. Resources are dedicated to addressing what is assumed to be a problem, and improvement is expected to follow.

item.title: Book
item.description:
Books that I've written

Writing is an often overlooked by vital component of solving problems, reducing costs, and improving quality. It records engineering judgement, and outlines how that judgement was formed. It is through writing that we come to better understand what we know and think we know.

The Virus of Variation

Making Sense of Death and Data Using Process Behavior Charts

Using the story of the 19th-century Hungarian physician, Ignaz Semmelweis, as a guide, The Virus of Variation teaches readers how to make sense of data using process behavior charts. Also known as control charts, process behavior charts are the only tool capable of making the invisible world of variation visible, allowing us to anticipate the future based on the past. This knowledge helps individuals and teams stop being reactive and start being proactive. It replaces luck with a math- and science-based methodology that reduces costs, improves quality, and, at least for Semmelweis, saves the lives of people in need.

item.title: BQI
item.description:
The Broken Quality Initiative

Helping engineers unlock the power of SPC

Most manufacturing efforts use conformance to specification as their guiding light. Rather than operate processes on-target with minimum variance—the definition of quality established by Dr. Genichi Taguchi in September 1960—quality, as defined in ISO 9000:2015 Clause 3.5.1, is defined as the degree to which a set of inherent characteristics of an object fulfills requirements.

While on its face this definition seems sensible—after all no customer in their right mind will accept product that does not fulfill requirements—it reinforces the perspective that quality is binary. It bolsters the widely held but wrong belief that the measured characteristics of parts, products, services, processes, and systems are either good or bad, conforming or nonconforming.

item.title: Essays
item.description:
Some essays that might be of interest

Essays exploring the theory and practice of data-driven problem solving, process behavior charts, and quality improvement in manufacturing. Click the respective card to read.

The Needle & the Cannula

This essay is a case study in the application of a novel Statistical Process Control (SPC) methodology called network analysis. The method uses a grid of process behavior charts to facilitate uninterrupted visual reasoning.

item.title: Presentations
item.description:
Public Speaking & Guest Lecturing

I am always looking for opportunities to speak with students and professionals. If you work with or manage a group that you think would benefit from an exporsure to my methods, reach out using the contact form at the bottom of this page or email me at James.Lehner@gmail.com.

The Challenge of Manufacturing

At its core, the challenge of manufacturing is the challenge of making parts, assemblies, and products that are, for all intents and purposes, the same. This is easier said than done because, as hard as we may try, no two parts, assemblies, or products will ever be exactly the same. Why? Because of something so ubiquitous that we tend to overlook it: variation.

item.title: Python
item.description:
process_improvement.py

A Python library dedicated to process improvement?
Just what I was looking for!

Learn more about the library on GitHub

The process_improvement.py library serves as a free alternative to tools like Excel, Minitab, and JMP, all of which require a fee to access. Assuming a rudimentary knowledge of Python, the library simplifies the calculations and generation of figures that play a foundational role in solving problems, reducing costs, and improving quality.

item.title: Web Apps
item.description:
Web Applications

Free tools, built by me (Jim Lehner), to start you on your journey of reducing costs and improving quality.

XmR Chart-It

The XmR Chart-It web app is a free-to-use XmR chart generating tool. It allows users to generate an XmR chart from a list of existing datasets or upload their own dataset as CSV. For those unfamiliar with the XmR chart, the app serves as a practical introduction to understanding variation through the lens of process behavior charts. For those familiar with it, it serves as a free alternative to pay-to-play software. Give it a try and let us know what you think!
